### Prerequisites

This text continues the previous text. There, we talked about the relationship between our knowledge and our certainties (<htcite0>). So, we suggest you study it before continuing.

### Introduction

In the first text of the Philosophy section, we studied how Aristotle understood knowledge. We saw that knowledge grows as we study. At some point, we realize it is not possible to know everything (<htcite0>).

We also learned something else: the more knowledge we have, the more we see that having many certainties can mean we still do not know many things (<htcite1>).

These facts lead us to some questions:

Reflection 1: On limits

Can we learn everything in school?

Or does school only provide us with the foundations to continue learning?

Upon graduating, does a person realize that there is much to learn? Or do most people think they have reached the final goal?

### A Russian game

As we study knowledge, we learn about a proposal by Doctor Francisco A. González Redondo. He says that, in school, students do not learn mathematics directly. They first learn a pre-mathematics and then a proto-mathematics. These are the first stages of learning. In one of his lectures, he even uses this idea for other areas of knowledge (<htcite0>; <htcite1>; <htcite2>; <htcite3>).

#### The answers

Doctor Francisco A. González Redondo agrees with Aristotle, who reached the same idea thousands of years ago. This idea tells us that, as we study, we can never master everything. On this path of knowledge, we start by making small discoveries with our own body. This is the pre phase. Next, as our knowledge grows, we add the earlier knowledge, but we still do not know everything. This is the proto phase. Finally, we begin to really understand a subject. At this stage, we see that there will always be a new horizon to explore.

This idea helps us answer the questions from **Reflection 1**: as our knowledge grows at school, we take the first steps to understand something bigger ahead. This will help us understand the universe around us better.

#### The Matryoshka (матрёшка)

What we study in this text can be shown by a toy made in Russia: the Matryoshka doll (*матрёшка*), as seen in **Graph 1**.

Graph 1: Matryoshka doll representing the stages of knowledge with the sum symbol (∑).

**Graph 1** shows exactly what happens as we study. When we start school, in Mathematics, we learn numbers and how to use them. This is the stage of the smallest doll. Doctor Francisco A. González Redondo calls this pre-mathematics. Next, we study proto-mathematics, the second doll. In this stage, we start to work with formulas, but we still do not prove them. Finally, when we enter college, a master's degree, or a doctorate, we add more knowledge. In this example, this is the third doll. Now our understanding gets closer to what happens in the world (<htcite0>; <htcite1>; <htcite2>).

The **Matryoshka** dolls are a good example of this growth of knowledge. The smaller dolls can fit inside the bigger ones. This shows that outer knowledge depends on inner knowledge. In other words, when we add layers of knowledge, we do not have an empty inside. Also, knowledge becomes stronger because of the layers.

This idea is not only about mathematics. We can use it in any area of knowledge. So, let us think more.

Reflection 2: Pre, proto, science and…

Initially, we spoke of three stages of learning: the pre-science, the proto-science and, finally, the science. But Graph 1 shows us four dolls.

What would this fourth doll mean?

We added the fourth doll to show that there is still more knowledge to gain, even when we know the sciences deeply. We can go further: nothing stops a fifth, a sixth, or more dolls from growing without limits.

### A toy to explain knowledge?

Often, when we grow up, we look at our past and see it as something that is over, something from other times. With this, we end up creating a barrier to new knowledge.

For example, a child would probably find it easy to keep adding dolls inside dolls while it is fun. An adult, on the other hand, may think they need to stop at some point, because they have other things to do.

Often, these everyday limits also make people create barriers for themselves. These barriers are not physical, like a wall. They are mental. Because of them, people tell themselves that they already know something, or that an idea is an unquestionable truth. As a result, these people cannot add another layer to their knowledge. Or, if you prefer, they do not add another outer doll to the previous dolls.

### Conclusion

In this text, we understood better what it means to know that we do not know.

We also studied more deeply the ideas of Doctor Francisco A. González Redondo about the stages we go through during our student life, until we reach knowledge in an area of science.

We learned all of this through a game. This shows that habits we left behind in childhood can still help us get new knowledge. Sometimes we do not get this knowledge because of the demands and tasks of everyday life.

exercise_v2.question: After leaving school, do we have complete mastery of all existing knowledge in the world?
exercise_v2.additionalInfo: School, as Doctor Francisco A. González Redondo mentions, helps us by offering an initial view of subjects, but does not necessarily deepen the concepts of a given area.

exercise_v2.question: Can habits we had in childhood help us acquire new knowledge?
exercise_v2.additionalInfo: Life often puts us in situations that end up creating barriers to learning new knowledge. Reviving some childhood habits, such as asking questions, helps us break through these barriers.
